analysis.one_liner: Cuts corporate tax rates and taxes on multinational income while adding new penalties for tax shelters and corporate expatriations.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill 24-15 and placed it on the House calendar, but the full House never voted before Congress ended; Congress passed a similar corporate tax package the next year.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite large parts of the corporate tax code: it would cap the corporate tax rate at 32% on income from domestic manufacturing, film, and construction, extend depreciation and expensing breaks, loosen a series of international tax rules for multinational companies, and repeal a disputed export subsidy (the extraterritorial income exclusion). It also contains real anti-avoidance provisions: new penalties for tax shelters, limits on companies that reincorporate overseas, and disclosure requirements for tax-shelter promoters. The bill was reported out of committee but never came to a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended in early 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the biggest winners are corporations: manufacturers and exporters get a lower 32% rate on domestic production income; multinational companies get easier international tax rules (simpler foreign tax credit baskets, repeal of foreign personal holding company and shipping income rules, treatment of the EU as one country); small corporations get lower rates and expanded expensing; and niche interests gain targeted breaks (distilled spirits wholesalers, restaurant and leasehold property owners, timber sellers, film exporters, cooperatives). The anti-avoidance provisions would also benefit honest taxpayers and the IRS by penalizing undisclosed tax shelters and corporate earnings-stripping.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the corporate tax rate at 32% (34% before 2007) on income from domestic manufacturing, qualified films, and U.S. construction and engineering services [S3][S4].
Reduces corporate rates for smaller corporations and extends increased small-business expensing through 2008 [S3].
Provides alternative minimum tax relief, including raising the gross-receipts exemption for small corporations from $7.5 million to $20 million [S3].

Loosens international tax rules for multinationals: treats EU member states as one country for certain rules, repeals foreign personal holding company and foreign base company shipping rules, reduces foreign tax credit categories from nine to two, and lets worldwide affiliated groups allocate interest expense as a single corporation [S3].

Adds anti-avoidance measures: penalties for failing to disclose reportable tax-shelter transactions, penalties on promoters and material advisers, tighter limits on earnings stripping, and an excise tax on insider stock compensation when companies expatriate [S2][S3].
Repeals the extraterritorial income exclusion, the export subsidy the World Trade Organization had ruled illegal, replacing it with the domestic production rate cut [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the lower corporate rates and international tax cuts, a cost ultimately shared by taxpayers generally through either foregone revenue or other taxes. Tax-shelter promoters, material advisers, and companies that inverted to foreign jurisdictions would face new penalties and taxes. Employees and executives with nonqualified deferred compensation plans would face stricter tax rules (a precursor of section 409A).

drawbacks.text: The revenue cost of cutting corporate rates and international taxes falls on the general taxpayer, with no offsetting revenue raised elsewhere in the bill [S2][S3].

The bill carries many narrow industry-specific favors — an income tax credit for distilled spirits wholesalers, suspension of occupational taxes on alcohol producers, repeal of the excise tax on sonar fish finders and fishing tackle boxes, 15-year depreciation for restaurant property — that are hard to defend as broad jobs policy [S3].

The label 'American Jobs Creation Act' covers a bill whose largest provisions are general corporate and multinational tax cuts; the connection to job creation is indirect and depends on companies investing the savings [S2][S3].
The new deferred compensation rules (section 409A) would impose complex compliance requirements on employer plans, with harsh results for participants when plans run afoul of them [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine mix, but tilted toward business tax cuts. Its anti-avoidance title — shelter penalties, disclosure requirements, limits on earnings stripping and expatriation — and the repeal of a WTO-illegal export subsidy served legitimate public purposes. But the bulk of the bill is a large package of corporate rate cuts, depreciation breaks, and international tax relaxations whose benefits flow overwhelmingly to companies and their shareholders, with the revenue cost spread across everyone else. The many narrow industry-specific tax breaks suggest a bill assembled as much for particular constituencies as for broad policy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Ways and Means Committee on a 24-15 vote and was placed on the House calendar in November 2003, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 — though Congress enacted a similar corporate tax package, the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004, through a separate bill.

narrative.text: Introduced July 25, 2003 by Rep. Bill Thomas and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee [S6].
The committee held a markup on October 28, 2003 and ordered the bill reported amended by a vote of 24-15 [S6].
The committee reported the amended bill on November 21, 2003 (H. Rept. 108-393) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 226 [S6][S4].
No further action was taken: the bill never received a vote on the House floor and died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because this bill itself never became law, its specific provisions never took effect; however, Congress enacted a substantially similar corporate tax package — the American Jobs Creation Act of 2004 — through separate legislation later the same year, so the corporate beneficiaries of this bill largely obtained what they wanted by a different route. Readers should treat the 2004 law as separate legislation with its own record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations, via the 2004 successor law

industries.note: The bill loosens a series of international tax rules — simpler foreign tax credit baskets, repeal of foreign personal holding company and shipping income rules, EU treated as one country — reducing taxes these companies pay, with the revenue cost borne by other taxpayers. The bill partly offsets this with tighter earnings-stripping rules.

A 32% cap on the corporate rate for domestic production income is a large tax cut for manufacturers, and repealing the WTO-illegal export subsidy protected U.S. exports from European retaliatory tariffs — a genuine benefit to export-sector workers as well as companies. The rate cut itself, however, is paid for by general revenue.

New penalties for failing to disclose reportable transactions, penalties on material advisers, and injunction authority target promoters of abusive tax shelters, which protects honest taxpayers who otherwise effectively subsidize evasion.

industries.industry: U.S. companies inverting to foreign incorporation
industries.note: The bill increases taxation of inversion transactions, limits earnings stripping, and imposes an excise tax on insider stock compensation in expatriated corporations — aimed at companies that reincorporate abroad to lower their U.S. taxes.

Suspends occupational taxes on producers and marketers of distilled spirits, wine, and beer for three years and gives distilled spirits wholesalers a credit for financing costs of the federal excise tax — targeted breaks for a specific industry.

S corporation banks and financial companies get expanded eligibility and exemptions from passive income tests, and the active financing exemption from subpart F is modified — tax benefits for the financial industry.

Income from qualified films exploited abroad is partially excluded from gross income, rising to 10% by 2013, plus the domestic production rate cap and expanded orphan drug credit — targeted benefits for Hollywood exporters.

Lower corporate rates, expanded expensing, S corporation rules allowing 100 shareholders and family elections, and AMT exemption expansion genuinely reduce the tax burden on smaller firms. Small businesses compete with larger ones, so these breaks also have distributional effects within the business community.
